claims.text: An integrated high-throughput ab initio molecular-dynamics and statistical-learning framework can accurately predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting across high-entropy alloys.
Single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni compositionally complex alloys can have predominantly FCC-based structures.
NiFeCoCr-based alloys in the proposed target set have predominantly FCC structures.
The targeted alloys are synthesized under ambient conditions.
First-principles Monte Carlo or molecular-dynamics simulations can determine chemical short-range order, bond-length distributions, and local lattice distortions in Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni alloys.
The cited simulation approach is suitable for high-throughput application across a broad HEA compositional landscape.
Regression models can map local lattice distortions and short-range-order metrics to melting and fusion properties.
Local bond-length distributions and lattice distortions influence the free-energy landscape of high-entropy alloys.
Changes in the free-energy landscape caused by local distortions and chemical short-range order modulate melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting.
Statistical models can capture correlations between local structural metrics and melting properties with useful predictive accuracy.
The integrated approach will predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change within approximately ±10% of experimental values.
The integrated approach will be more accurate and efficient than traditional experiments or simple empirical models.
Traditional experimental characterization and simple empirical models have larger uncertainties and are less efficient for exploring HEA compositional space.
The claimed predictive accuracy applies primarily to single-phase, FCC-based high-entropy alloys.
Predictive accuracy may decline in alloys with substantial secondary phases, non-equilibrium phases, or compositions far outside the model's calibration range.
Prior work has correlated local lattice distortions with a macroscale property using a linear regression model.
Prior work has established correlations between local lattice distortions and macroscale melting or fusion thermodynamic properties.
DSC, calorimetry, and dilatometry can provide the experimental melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and melting volume change needed for validation.
Deviation greater than ±10% for a significant number of tested alloys, or absence of a statistically significant mediator–property correlation, is designated as a falsifying result.
